title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Conclusion of the Mercantile System

Encouraging exports and discouraging imports are the two great engines the mercantile system relies on to enrich a country. Yet for certain commodities it does the reverse: it discourages export and encourages import. The system insists, though, that its ultimate aim never changes—to enrich the country through a favourable balance of trade. So it discourages exporting the raw materials of manufacture and the tools of trade, hoping to give our own workmen an edge and let them undersell foreign workers in every overseas market; by holding back the export of a few low-priced goods in this way, it expects to generate a much larger and more valuable export of other goods. It encourages importing the raw materials of manufacture so that our own people can work them up more cheaply, and so prevent a larger and more valuable import of finished goods. I notice no encouragement, at least in our statute book, for importing the tools of trade. Once manufacturing reaches a certain scale, making those tools becomes itself the business of many important industries, and giving any special encouragement to importing such tools would clash too much with the interests of those industries. So instead of being encouraged, such imports have often been banned outright. The import of wool cards, for instance—except from Ireland, or when they came in as wreckage or as prize goods—was banned by the 3rd of Edward IV; that ban was renewed by the 39th of Elizabeth, and later laws kept it in force and made it permanent.
Importing the raw materials of manufacture has sometimes been encouraged by exempting them from the duties other goods must pay, and sometimes by bounties.

The import of sheep's wool from several different countries, of cotton wool from every country, of undressed flax, of most dyeing drugs, of most undressed hides from Ireland or the British colonies, of seal skins from the British Greenland fishery, of pig and bar iron from the British colonies, along with several other raw materials of manufacture, has been encouraged by exempting them from all duties—provided they are properly entered at the custom-house. The self-interest of our merchants and manufacturers may have wrung these exemptions out of the legislature, just as it produced most of our other commercial regulations. Even so, the exemptions are perfectly fair and reasonable; and if the needs of the state allowed them to be extended to all the other raw materials of manufacture, the public would surely gain.

The greed of our great manufacturers, however, has in some cases stretched these exemptions well beyond what can fairly count as the raw materials of their trade. Under the 24th George II, chapter 46, a small duty of only 1d a pound was placed on imported foreign brown linen yarn, replacing much higher duties it had carried before: 6d a pound on sail yarn, 1s a pound on all French and Dutch yarn, and £2:13:4 on every hundredweight of spruce or Muscovia yarn. But our manufacturers were not satisfied with this reduction for long. Under the 29th of the same king, chapter 15—the very law that granted a bounty on exporting British and Irish linen priced at no more than 18d a yard—even this small duty on imported brown linen yarn was abolished. Yet the various steps needed to prepare linen yarn employ a good deal more labour than the later step of making linen cloth from that yarn. Setting aside the work of the flax-growers and flax-dressers, at least three or four spinners are needed to keep one weaver continuously busy; more than four-fifths of all the labour required to produce linen cloth goes into producing the yarn. But our spinners are poor people—women, usually scattered across all parts of the country, with no support or protection. Our great master manufacturers make their profits not by selling the spinners' work but by selling the weavers' finished product. Since it is in their interest to sell the finished manufacture as dear as possible, it is equally in their interest to buy the materials as cheap as possible. By wringing from the legislature bounties on exporting their own linen, high duties on importing all foreign linen, and an outright ban on home consumption of certain kinds of French linen, they try to sell their own goods as dear as possible. By encouraging the import of foreign linen yarn, and so setting it in competition with the yarn our own people make, they try to buy the poor spinners' work as cheap as possible. They are just as set on keeping down their own weavers' wages as on keeping down the spinners' earnings; and they raise the price of the finished work, or lower the price of the raw materials, in no way for the workers' benefit. It is the industry carried on for the benefit of the rich and powerful that our mercantile system mainly encourages. The industry carried on for the benefit of the poor and the needy is too often either neglected or oppressed.

Both the bounty on exporting linen and the exemption from the duty on imported foreign yarn were granted for only fifteen years; but, extended twice, they run until the end of the parliamentary session that immediately follows the 24th of June 1786.
The encouragement given by bounties to importing the raw materials of manufacture has been confined mainly to materials brought in from our American plantations.

The first bounties of this kind were granted around the start of the present century, on importing naval stores from America. That term covered timber fit for masts, yards, and bowsprits, along with hemp, tar, pitch, and turpentine. The bounty of £1 a ton on masting-timber, and of £6 a ton on hemp, was also extended to such goods imported into England from Scotland. Both bounties continued unchanged at the same rate until each was allowed to lapse: the one on hemp on the 1st of January 1741, and the one on masting-timber at the end of the parliamentary session immediately following the 24th of June 1781.

The bounties on importing tar, pitch, and turpentine were altered several times while they lasted. Originally the bounty on tar was £4 a ton, on pitch the same, and on turpentine £3 a ton. The £4 bounty on tar was later restricted to tar prepared in a particular way; the bounty on other good, clean, merchantable tar was cut to £2:4s a ton. The bounty on pitch was likewise cut to £1, and the one on turpentine to £1:10s a ton.

The second bounty on importing any raw material of manufacture, in order of time, was granted by the 21st George II, chapter 30, on importing indigo from the British plantations. When plantation indigo was worth three-fourths of the price of the best French indigo, this act entitled it to a bounty of 6d a pound. Like most bounties, it was granted only for a limited time; it was continued by several extensions but reduced to 4d a pound. It was allowed to lapse at the end of the parliamentary session following the 25th of March 1781.

The third bounty of this kind was granted—right around the time we were beginning sometimes to court and sometimes to quarrel with our American colonies—by the 4th George III, chapter 26, on importing hemp or undressed flax from the British plantations. It ran for twenty-one years, from the 24th of June 1764 to the 24th of June 1785. For the first seven years it was £8 a ton; for the second seven, £6; for the third seven, £4. It was not extended to Scotland, whose climate (although hemp is sometimes grown there in small quantities and of inferior quality) is not well suited to that crop. A bounty on importing Scotch flax into England would have discouraged the native produce of the southern part of the United Kingdom too severely.

The fourth bounty of this kind was granted by the 5th George III, chapter 45, on importing wood from America. It ran for nine years, from the 1st of January 1766 to the 1st of January 1775. During the first three years it was £1 for every hundred-and-twenty good deals, and 12s for every load of fifty cubic feet of other squared timber. During the second three years it was 15s for deals and 8s for other squared timber; and during the third three years it was 10s for deals and 5s for every other squared timber.

The fifth bounty of this kind was granted by the 9th George III, chapter 38, on importing raw silk from the British plantations. It ran for twenty-one years, from the 1st of January 1770 to the 1st of January 1791. For the first seven years it was £25 for every hundred pounds of value; for the second seven, £20; for the third seven, £15. Managing the silkworm and preparing silk takes so much hand-labour, and labour is so dear in America, that even this large bounty was, I am told, unlikely to have much effect.

The sixth bounty of this kind was granted by the 11th George III, chapter 50, on importing pipe, hogshead, and barrel staves and heading from the British plantations. It ran for nine years, from the 1st of January 1772 to the 1st of January 1781. For the first three years it was £6 for a certain quantity of each; for the second three years, £4; for the third three years, £2.

The seventh and last bounty of this kind was granted by the 19th George III, chapter 37, on importing hemp from Ireland. It was framed just like the bounty for importing hemp and undressed flax from America: for twenty-one years, from the 24th of June 1779 to the 24th of June 1800. Its term is likewise split into three periods of seven years each, and in each period the Irish rate matches the American one. Unlike the American bounty, though, it does not cover importing undressed flax, since that would have discouraged growing the plant in Great Britain too much. When this last bounty was granted, the British and Irish legislatures were in no better humour with each other than the British and American had been before. But this gift to Ireland, one hopes, was granted under more fortunate stars than all those granted to America. The same goods on which we gave these bounties when imported from America carried heavy duties when imported from any other country. The interest of our American colonies was treated as identical to that of the mother country. Their wealth was counted as our wealth. Whatever money was sent out to them, people said, all came back to us through the balance of trade, so no expense laid out on them could ever leave us a farthing poorer. They were ours in every respect, and the spending was treated as money laid out improving our own property and gainfully employing our own people. I think there is no need now to say anything more to expose the folly of a system that bitter experience has by now exposed thoroughly enough. Had our American colonies really been part of Great Britain, those bounties might have counted as bounties on production, and they would still have carried every objection such bounties carry—but no other.
Exporting the raw materials of manufacture is sometimes discouraged by outright bans, and sometimes by high duties.

Our woollen manufacturers have been more successful than any other class of workmen at convincing the legislature that the nation's prosperity hinges on the success and expansion of their particular trade. They have not only won a monopoly against consumers, through an outright ban on importing woollen cloth from any foreign country; they have also won a second monopoly against the sheep farmers and wool growers, through a matching ban on exporting live sheep and wool. Many of the laws passed to protect the revenue are rightly criticised for imposing heavy penalties on acts that, before the statutes declared them crimes, had always been regarded as innocent. But I will go so far as to say that even our cruellest revenue laws are mild and gentle compared with some of the laws our merchants' and manufacturers' clamour has wrung from the legislature to prop up their own absurd and oppressive monopolies. Like the laws of Draco, these laws may be said to be written entirely in blood.

Under the 8th of Elizabeth, chapter 3, anyone who exported sheep, lambs, or rams was, for the first offence, to forfeit all his goods forever, suffer a year's imprisonment, and then have his left hand cut off in a market town on a market day and nailed up there; for the second offence, he was to be judged a felon and put to death accordingly. The aim of this law seems to have been to stop our breed of sheep from spreading to foreign countries. Under the 13th and 14th of Charles II, chapter 18, exporting wool was made a felony, and the exporter faced the same penalties and forfeitures as any felon.

For the honour of our national humanity, one hopes neither of these statutes was ever carried out. The first, however, has so far as I know never been directly repealed, and Serjeant Hawkins seems to treat it as still in force. It may perhaps be considered as repealed in effect by the 12th of Charles II, chapter 32, section 3, which—without expressly removing the penalties set by earlier statutes—imposes a new penalty: 20s for every sheep exported or attempted to be exported, plus forfeiture of the sheep and of the owner's share in them. The second statute was expressly repealed by the 7th and 8th of William III, chapter 28, section 4, which declares: "Whereas the statute of the 13th and 14th of King Charles II made against the exportation of wool, among other things in the said act mentioned, doth enact the same to be deemed felony, by the severity of which penalty the prosecution of offenders hath not been so effectually put in execution; be it therefore enacted, by the authority aforesaid, that so much of the said act, which relates to the making the said offence felony, be repealed and made void."

The penalties left in place—whether imposed by this milder statute or carried over from earlier ones it does not repeal—are still harsh enough. Besides forfeiting the goods, the exporter incurs a penalty of 3s for every pound weight of wool exported or attempted to be exported, which is roughly four or five times its value. Any merchant or other person convicted of the offence loses the right to recover any debt or account owed to him by any agent or other person. Whatever his fortune, and whether or not he can pay these heavy penalties, the law intends to ruin him completely. But since the morals of the bulk of the people are not yet as corrupt as those of the men who devised this statute, I have not heard of anyone ever exploiting this clause. If the person convicted cannot pay the penalties within three months of judgment, he is to be transported for seven years; and if he returns before that term is up, he faces the penalties of felony without benefit of clergy. A ship's owner who knows of the offence forfeits his entire interest in the ship and its furnishings. The master and mariners who know of it forfeit all their goods and chattels and serve three months' imprisonment. By a later statute, the master serves six months' imprisonment.

To prevent export, the whole inland trade in wool is placed under very heavy and oppressive restrictions. Wool cannot be packed in any box, barrel, cask, case, chest, or other container, but only in packs of leather or pack-cloth, on which the word WOOL or YARN must be marked on the outside in large letters at least three inches long, on pain of forfeiting both the wool and the package, plus 8s for every pound weight, payable by the owner or packer. It cannot be loaded onto any horse or cart, or carried by land within five miles of the coast, except between sunrise and sunset, on pain of forfeiting the wool, the horses, and the carriages. The hundred next to the sea coast, out of or through which the wool is carried or exported, forfeits £20 if the wool is worth under £10, and if worth more, treble that value plus treble costs, to be sued for within the year. Enforcement falls on any two of the inhabitants, whom the sessions must repay through an assessment on the others, just as in cases of robbery. And if anyone settles with the hundred for less than this penalty, he is to be imprisoned for five years, and any other person may prosecute. These rules apply throughout the whole kingdom.

But in the particular counties of Kent and Sussex the restrictions are even more troublesome. Every wool owner within ten miles of the sea coast must give a written account, within three days of shearing, to the nearest customs officer, stating how many fleeces he has and where they are kept. Before he moves any of them, he must again give notice of the number and weight of the fleeces, the name and home of the buyer, and the place to which they are to be carried. No one within fifteen miles of the sea in those counties may buy any wool until he has bound himself to the king that none of the wool he buys will be sold by him to any other person within fifteen miles of the sea. If any wool is found being carried toward the sea in those counties without having been entered and secured as above, it is forfeited, and the offender also forfeits 3s for every pound weight. If anyone keeps any wool, not entered as above, within fifteen miles of the sea, it must be seized and forfeited; and if anyone claims it after seizure, he must give security to the exchequer that, if he loses at trial, he will pay treble costs on top of all other penalties.

When such restrictions burden the inland trade, we can be sure the coasting trade is not left very free either. Every wool owner who carries, or has carried, any wool to any port or place on the sea coast, intending to ship it by sea to another place or port on the coast, must first have an entry made at the port it is to leave from, listing the weight, marks, and number of the packages, before bringing it within five miles of that port—on pain of forfeiting the wool, along with the horses, carts, and other vehicles, and of suffering the forfeitures of the other laws in force against exporting wool. This law (the 1st of William III, chapter 32) is, however, so indulgent as to declare that it shall not stop anyone from carrying his wool home from the place of shearing, even within five miles of the sea, provided that within ten days of shearing, and before he moves it, he certifies under his own hand to the nearest customs officer the true number of fleeces and where they are housed, and does not move them without certifying his intention to that officer, under his hand, three days beforehand. Bond must be given that wool carried by sea will be landed at the particular port for which it was entered outward; and if any of it is landed without an officer present, not only is the wool forfeited, as with other goods, but the usual extra penalty of 3s for every pound weight is incurred as well.

To justify their demand for such extraordinary restrictions, our woollen manufacturers confidently claimed that English wool was of a special quality, superior to that of any other country; that the wool of other countries could not be worked into any decent fabric without some of it mixed in; that fine cloth could not be made without it; that England, therefore, if its export could be entirely stopped, could corner almost the whole woollen trade of the world; and that, having no rivals, she could then sell at whatever price she liked and quickly amass incredible wealth through the most favourable balance of trade. Like most doctrines confidently asserted by a sizeable group, this one was, and still is, implicitly believed by a far larger group—by nearly everyone who either knows nothing of the woollen trade or has never looked into it closely. Yet it is so utterly false that English wool is in any way necessary for making fine cloth that it is actually unfit for it. Fine cloth is made entirely from Spanish wool. English wool cannot even be mixed with Spanish wool without spoiling and degrading, to some degree, the fabric of the cloth.

An earlier part of this work has shown that the effect of these regulations has been to depress the price of English wool not only below what it would naturally be today, but far below what it actually was in the time of Edward III. Scotch wool, once it came under the same regulations through the Union, is said to have fallen by about half. The very accurate and intelligent author of the Memoirs of Wool, the Reverend Mr John Smith, observes that the price of the best English wool in England is generally below what wool of much lower quality usually fetches in the Amsterdam market. The avowed purpose of these regulations was to push the price of this commodity below what might be called its natural and proper level, and there seems no doubt they produced the effect expected of them.

It might be thought that this drop in price, by discouraging wool-growing, must have greatly cut the annual output of wool—if not below its former level, then below what it would probably have reached in present conditions, had an open and free market let it rise to its natural and proper price. I am inclined to believe, however, that the quantity of annual output cannot have been much affected by these regulations, though it may have been affected a little. Growing wool is not the main reason the sheep farmer puts his work and capital into the trade. He expects his profit not so much from the price of the fleece as from the price of the carcase, and the average or ordinary price of the carcase must, in many cases, make up for whatever shortfall there is in the average or ordinary price of the fleece. As an earlier part of this work observed: "whatever regulations tend to sink the price, either of wool or of raw hides, below what it naturally would be, must, in an improved and cultivated country, have some tendency to raise the price of butcher's meat. The price, both of the great and small cattle which are fed on improved and cultivated land, must be sufficient to pay the rent which the landlord, and the profit which the farmer, has reason to expect from improved and cultivated land. If it is not, they will soon cease to feed them. Whatever part of this price, therefore, is not paid by the wool and the hide, must be paid by the carcase. The less there is paid for the one, the more must be paid for the other. In what manner this price is to be divided upon the different parts of the beast, is indifferent to the landlords and farmers, provided it is all paid to them. In an improved and cultivated country, therefore, their interest as landlords and farmers cannot be much affected by such regulations, though their interest as consumers may, by the rise in the price of provisions." By this reasoning, then, the lowering of the wool price is unlikely, in an improved and cultivated country, to cause any drop in the annual output of wool—except insofar as, by raising the price of mutton, it may slightly reduce the demand for, and so the production of, that particular kind of butcher's meat. Even in this respect, its effect is probably not very great.

But while its effect on the quantity of annual output may not have been very great, one might suppose its effect on the quality must have been very great indeed. The decline in the quality of English wool—if not below its former level, then below what it would naturally have reached in the present state of improvement and cultivation—might be supposed to be very nearly in proportion to the decline in price. Since quality depends on the breed, the pasture, and the management and cleanliness of the sheep throughout the growth of the fleece, one might naturally imagine that the attention paid to these things can never be greater than the reward the fleece's price is likely to give for the labour and expense that attention requires. As it happens, though, the goodness of the fleece depends largely on the health, growth, and size of the animal: the same attention needed to improve the carcase is, in some measure, enough to improve the fleece too. Despite the fall in price, English wool is said to have improved considerably even over the course of the present century. The improvement might perhaps have been greater had the price been better; but the low price, though it may have hampered that improvement, has certainly not prevented it altogether.

The harshness of these regulations, then, seems to have affected neither the quantity nor the quality of the annual wool output as much as might have been expected (though I think it likely the quality has been affected a good deal more than the quantity); and the interest of the wool growers, though it must have been harmed to some degree, seems on the whole to have been hurt far less than one might easily have imagined.
These considerations, however, will not justify an outright ban on exporting wool; but they fully justify imposing a considerable tax on that export.

To harm, in any degree, the interest of one class of citizens for no purpose but to advance that of another plainly violates the justice and equal treatment a sovereign owes to all the different classes of his subjects. Yet the ban certainly does harm, to some degree, the interest of the wool growers, for no purpose but to advance that of the manufacturers.

Every class of citizens is bound to help support the sovereign or the commonwealth. A tax of five, or even ten, shillings on every tod of wool exported would yield the sovereign a considerable revenue. It would hurt the growers somewhat less than the ban does, because it probably would not lower the wool price quite so much. It would give the manufacturer a sufficient advantage too, because although he might not buy his wool quite as cheaply as under the ban, he would still buy it at least five or ten shillings cheaper than any foreign manufacturer could—besides saving the freight and insurance the foreigner would have to pay. It is hard to imagine a tax that could raise the sovereign a sizeable revenue while causing so little inconvenience to anyone.

The ban, for all the penalties guarding it, does not stop wool from being exported. It is well known that wool is exported in great quantities. The wide gap between the home price and the foreign price offers such a temptation to smuggling that all the law's severity cannot prevent it. This illegal export benefits no one but the smuggler. A legal export, subject to a tax, would yield the sovereign a revenue and so spare him the need to impose some other tax, perhaps more burdensome and inconvenient; it might prove advantageous to all the different subjects of the state.

The export of fuller's earth, or fuller's clay—thought necessary for preparing and cleansing woollen manufactures—has been subjected to nearly the same penalties as the export of wool. Even tobacco-pipe clay, though admittedly different from fuller's clay, has been placed under the same bans and penalties, because of their resemblance and because fuller's clay might sometimes be exported disguised as tobacco-pipe clay.

By the 13th and 14th of Charles II, chapter 7, the export not only of raw hides but of tanned leather—except in the form of boots, shoes, or slippers—was banned; and the law granted a monopoly to our boot-makers and shoe-makers, not only against our graziers but against our tanners. By later statutes our tanners got themselves exempted from this monopoly, on paying a small tax of just one shilling on the hundredweight of tanned leather weighing one hundred and twelve pounds. They have also obtained a drawback of two-thirds of the excise duties on their goods, even when exported without further manufacture. All leather manufactures may be exported duty-free, and the exporter is also entitled to a drawback of the whole excise duties. Our graziers, meanwhile, remain subject to the old monopoly. Graziers, separated from one another and dispersed through every corner of the country, cannot easily combine to impose monopolies on their fellow citizens or to free themselves from monopolies others have imposed on them. Manufacturers of every kind, gathered in large numbers in all the great cities, can easily do so. Even the horns of cattle are banned from export, and the two trivial trades of horner and comb-maker enjoy, in this respect, a monopoly against the graziers.

Restraints—whether by bans or by taxes—on exporting goods that are partly but not fully manufactured are not unique to the leather trade. As long as anything still remains to be done to make a commodity ready for immediate use, our manufacturers think they themselves ought to be the ones doing it. Woollen yarn and worsted are banned from export under the same penalties as wool; even white cloths carry a duty on export, and our dyers have thereby won a monopoly against our clothiers. Our clothiers would probably have been able to resist this, but it happens that most of our leading clothiers are dyers themselves. Watch-cases, clock-cases, and dial-plates for clocks and watches have been banned from export. Our clock-makers and watch-makers, it seems, are unwilling to let foreign competition raise the price of this kind of workmanship against them.

By some old statutes of Edward III, Henry VIII, and Edward VI, the export of all metals was banned. Lead and tin alone were excepted, probably because those metals were so abundant—their export then made up a considerable part of the kingdom's trade. To encourage the mining trade, the 5th of William and Mary, chapter 17, exempted iron, copper, and mundic metal made from British ore from this ban. The export of all sorts of copper bars, foreign as well as British, was later allowed by the 9th and 10th of William III, chapter 26. The export of unmanufactured brass—what is called gun-metal, bell-metal, and shroff metal—is still banned. Brass manufactures of all sorts may be exported duty-free.
Where the export of the raw materials of manufacture is not banned outright, it is in many cases subjected to considerable duties.

By the 8th George I, chapter 15, the export of all goods produced or manufactured in Great Britain, on which earlier statutes had laid any duties, was made duty-free. The following goods, however, were excepted: alum, lead, lead-ore, tin, tanned leather, copperas, coals, wool, cards, white woollen cloths, lapis calaminaris, skins of all sorts, glue, coney hair or wool, hares' wool, hair of all sorts, horses, and litharge of lead. Apart from horses, all of these are either raw materials of manufacture, or incomplete manufactures (which can be treated as materials for still further manufacture), or tools of trade. This statute leaves them subject to all the old duties ever imposed on them—the old subsidy, and one per cent outward.

By the same statute, a great many foreign drugs used by dyers are exempted from all import duties. Each of them, however, is then subjected to a certain duty—not a very heavy one—on export. Our dyers, it seems, while they judged it in their interest to encourage importing those drugs by exempting them from all duties, also judged it in their interest to put some small discouragement on exporting them. But the greed behind this notable piece of mercantile cleverness most likely defeated its own purpose. It inevitably taught importers to be more careful than they might otherwise have been not to import more than the home market needed. The home market was therefore always likely to be more thinly supplied, and these commodities always likely to be somewhat dearer there than they would have been had export been made as free as import.

By the same statute, gum senega, or gum arabic, being among the listed dyeing drugs, could be imported duty-free. It carried only a small poundage duty, amounting to just threepence in the hundredweight, on re-export. France enjoyed at that time an exclusive trade with the country most productive of these drugs—the country near the Senegal—and the British market could not easily be supplied by importing them directly from where they grew. So by the 25th George II, gum senega was allowed to be imported (contrary to the general terms of the act of navigation) from any part of Europe. But since the law did not mean to encourage this kind of trade, so contrary to the general principles of England's mercantile policy, it placed a duty of ten shillings the hundredweight on such imports, and none of this duty was to be drawn back on export. The successful war that began in 1755 gave Great Britain the same exclusive trade with those countries that France had enjoyed before. As soon as peace came, our manufacturers tried to exploit this advantage and to set up a monopoly in their own favour, both against the growers and against the importers of this commodity. So by the 5th George III, chapter 37, the export of gum senega from his majesty's dominions in Africa was confined to Great Britain, and was placed under all the same restrictions, regulations, forfeitures, and penalties as the listed commodities of the British colonies in America and the West Indies. Its import, indeed, carried only a small duty of sixpence the hundredweight, but its re-export carried the enormous duty of one pound ten shillings the hundredweight. Our manufacturers intended that the whole produce of those countries should be imported into Great Britain, and—so they could buy it at their own price—that none of it should be exported again except at a cost high enough to discourage that export thoroughly. But their greed, here as on many other occasions, defeated its own purpose. This enormous duty offered such a temptation to smuggling that great quantities of the commodity were smuggled out—probably to all the manufacturing countries of Europe, but especially to Holland—not only from Great Britain but from Africa. On this account, by the 14th George III, chapter 10, the export duty was cut to five shillings the hundredweight.

In the book of rates by which the old subsidy was levied, beaver skins were valued at six shillings and eightpence apiece; and the various subsidies and imposts laid on their import before the year 1722 came to one-fifth of that rate, or sixteen pence per skin—all of which, except half the old subsidy (only twopence), was drawn back on export. This import duty on so important a raw material of manufacture had been thought too high; and in 1722 the rate was cut to two shillings and sixpence, which reduced the import duty to sixpence, and of this only half was to be drawn back on export. The same successful war put the country most productive of beaver under British rule; and since beaver skins were among the listed commodities, their export from America was accordingly confined to the British market. Our manufacturers soon saw the advantage they could make of this, and in 1764 the import duty on beaver skin was cut to one penny, while the export duty was raised to sevenpence per skin, with no drawback of the import duty. By the same law, a duty of eighteen pence a pound was laid on the export of beaver wool or woumbs, with no change to the import duty on that commodity, which, when imported by British subjects in British shipping, then came to between fourpence and fivepence the piece.

Coals can be regarded both as a raw material of manufacture and as a tool of trade. Heavy duties, accordingly, have been placed on their export, amounting at present (1783) to more than five shillings the ton, or more than fifteen shillings the chaldron, Newcastle measure—which in most cases is more than the original value of the coal at the pit, or even at the port from which it is shipped for export.

The export of the tools of trade proper, however, is usually held back not by high duties but by outright bans. Thus, by the 7th and 8th of William III, chapter 20, section 8, the export of frames or engines for knitting gloves or stockings is banned, under the penalty not only of forfeiting any such frames or engines exported or attempted to be exported, but of forty pounds—half to the king, half to whoever informs or sues for it. In the same way, by the 14th George III, chapter 71, the export to foreign parts of any tools used in the cotton, linen, woollen, and silk manufactures is banned, under the penalty not only of forfeiting the tools but of two hundred pounds payable by the offender, and a further two hundred pounds payable by the master of the ship who knowingly lets such tools be loaded aboard.

When such heavy penalties were placed on exporting the dead tools of trade, the living tool—the skilled worker—could hardly be expected to go free. Accordingly, by the 5th George I, chapter 27, anyone convicted of enticing any artificer in any of the manufactures of Great Britain to go abroad to practise or teach his trade is liable, for the first offence, to a fine of up to one hundred pounds and three months' imprisonment, and to remain imprisoned until the fine is paid; and for the second offence, to a fine at the court's discretion and twelve months' imprisonment, again until the fine is paid. By the 23rd George II, chapter 13, this penalty is raised: for the first offence, to five hundred pounds for every artificer so enticed and twelve months' imprisonment, until the fine is paid; and for the second offence, to one thousand pounds and two years' imprisonment, until the fine is paid.

By the first of these two statutes, upon proof that anyone has been enticing an artificer, or that an artificer has promised or agreed to go abroad for the purposes described, the artificer may be required to give security, at the court's discretion, that he will not go overseas, and may be committed to prison until he gives that security.

If an artificer has gone overseas and is practising or teaching his trade in a foreign country, then upon being warned by any of his majesty's ministers or consuls abroad, or by one of his majesty's secretaries of state for the time being, he must, within six months of that warning, return to this realm and from then on stay and live continually within it. If he does not, he is from that point declared unable to take any legacy left to him within this kingdom, to act as executor or administrator to anyone, or to take any land within this kingdom by descent, devise, or purchase. He also forfeits to the king all his land, goods, and chattels; is declared an alien in every respect; and is put outside the king's protection.

There is no need, I imagine, to point out how contrary such regulations are to the boasted liberty of the subject, of which we pretend to be so jealous—yet which, in this case, is plainly sacrificed to the petty interests of our merchants and manufacturers.

The supposedly praiseworthy aim of all these regulations is to expand our own manufactures—not by improving them, but by depressing those of all our neighbours, and by putting an end, as far as possible, to the troublesome competition of such hateful and disagreeable rivals. Our master manufacturers think it reasonable that they alone should have a monopoly on the ingenuity of all their countrymen. By limiting, in some trades, the number of apprentices that can be employed at one time, and by requiring a long apprenticeship in all trades, they all try to confine the knowledge of their respective callings to as few people as possible; yet they are unwilling to let any of even that small number go abroad to instruct foreigners.
Consumption is the sole end and purpose of all production, and the producer's interest ought to be attended to only so far as it serves the consumer's.

The maxim is so completely self-evident that it would be absurd to try to prove it. But in the mercantile system the consumer's interest is almost constantly sacrificed to the producer's, and the system seems to treat production, not consumption, as the ultimate end and object of all industry and commerce.

In the restraints on importing any foreign commodity that could compete with what we ourselves grow or make, the home consumer's interest is plainly sacrificed to the producer's. It is entirely for the producer's benefit that the consumer is made to pay the higher price this monopoly almost always causes.

It is entirely for the producer's benefit that bounties are granted on exporting some of his goods. The home consumer is made to pay, first, the tax needed to fund the bounty, and second, the still larger tax that inevitably arises from the higher price of the commodity in the home market.

By the famous treaty of commerce with Portugal, duties stop the consumer from buying, from a neighbouring country, a commodity our own climate does not produce; instead he is forced to buy it from a distant country, even though it is admitted that the distant country's commodity is of worse quality than the nearer one's. The home consumer is made to put up with this inconvenience so that the producer may export some of his own goods into the distant country on better terms than he would otherwise have been allowed. And the consumer is also made to pay whatever rise in the price of those very goods this forced export causes in the home market.

But in the system of laws set up to manage our American and West Indian colonies, the home consumer's interest has been sacrificed to the producer's with even more extravagant profusion than in all our other commercial regulations. A great empire has been built for the sole purpose of raising up a nation of customers obliged to buy, from the shops of our various producers, all the goods these producers could supply. For the sake of the small rise in price this monopoly might give our producers, the home consumers have been saddled with the whole expense of maintaining and defending that empire. For this purpose, and this purpose alone, more than two hundred millions have been spent in the two last wars, and a new debt of more than a hundred and seventy millions has been contracted, on top of everything spent for the same purpose in earlier wars. The interest on this debt alone is not only greater than the whole extra profit that could ever even be claimed for the monopoly of the colony trade, but greater than the entire value of that trade—greater than the whole value of the goods exported, on average, to the colonies each year.

It cannot be very hard to work out who designed this whole mercantile system. Not the consumers, we may be sure, whose interest has been entirely neglected; but the producers, whose interest has been so carefully looked after—and among them, our merchants and manufacturers have been by far the chief architects. In the mercantile regulations dealt with in this chapter, it is the interest of our manufacturers that has been most particularly attended to; and the interest sacrificed to it has been not so much that of the consumers as that of certain other sets of producers.

title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Agricultural Systems, or Those Systems of Political Economy That Treat the Produce of Land as Either the Sole or the Principal Source of Every Country's Revenue and Wealth
The agricultural systems of political economy will not need as long an explanation as the one I thought necessary to give the mercantile or commercial system.

As far as I know, no nation has ever adopted the system that treats the produce of land as the sole source of a country's revenue and wealth. At present it exists only in the theories of a few very learned and ingenious men in France. Surely it would not be worth examining at length the errors of a system that has never done, and probably never will do, any harm anywhere in the world. Still, I will try to lay out the broad outlines of this very ingenious system as clearly as I can.

Mr Colbert, the famous minister of Louis XIV, was a man of integrity, great diligence, and command of detail. He had wide experience and a sharp eye for examining public accounts, and in short he had every ability needed to bring method and good order into the collection and spending of public revenue. Unfortunately, that minister had taken on all the prejudices of the mercantile system, which is by its very nature a system of restraint and regulation. Such a system could hardly fail to appeal to a hard-working, plodding man of business, used to managing the various departments of public offices and setting up the checks and controls needed to keep each one within its proper sphere. He tried to regulate the industry and commerce of a great country on the same model as the departments of a public office. Instead of letting every man pursue his own interest in his own way, on the liberal plan of equality, liberty, and justice, he granted special privileges to certain branches of industry while loading others with equally special restraints. Like other European ministers, he was inclined to favour the industry of the towns over that of the countryside; but he went further, and to prop up the towns' industry he was willing even to suppress and hold down that of the country. To make provisions cheap for townspeople, and so encourage manufactures and foreign trade, he banned the export of corn altogether, and thereby shut country people out of every foreign market for by far the most important part of what they produced. This ban, combined with the old provincial laws of France that restricted moving corn from one province to another, and with the arbitrary and degrading taxes levied on cultivators in almost every province, discouraged and held down French agriculture far below the level it would naturally have reached in such fertile soil and such a favourable climate. This state of discouragement and depression was felt to some degree in every part of the country, and many separate inquiries were launched into its causes. One of those causes appeared to be the preference that Mr Colbert's institutions gave to the industry of the towns over that of the country.

If a rod has been bent too far one way, the proverb says, you have to bend it just as far the other way to make it straight. The French philosophers who put forward the system that treats agriculture as the sole source of every country's revenue and wealth seem to have adopted this proverbial rule. Just as Mr Colbert's plan certainly overvalued the industry of the towns compared with that of the country, so their system seems to undervalue it just as surely.

They divide the different orders of people who have ever been supposed to contribute in any way to the country's yearly produce of land and labour into three classes. The first is the class of landowners. The second is the class of cultivators, farmers, and country labourers, whom they honour with the special name of the productive class. The third is the class of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants, whom they try to demean with the humiliating name of the barren or unproductive class.

The class of proprietors contributes to the yearly produce through whatever they may spend from time to time on improving the land: the buildings, drains, fences, and other betterments they make or maintain on it. By these means, the cultivators are able to raise a greater produce with the same capital, and so to pay a greater rent. This higher rent can be seen as the interest or profit due to the proprietor on the money or capital he puts into improving his land. In this system such outlays are called ground expenses (dépenses foncières).

The cultivators or farmers contribute to the yearly produce through what this system calls original and annual expenses (dépenses primitives et dépenses annuelles), which they lay out on cultivating the land. The original expenses consist of farming tools, the stock of cattle, the seed, and the upkeep of the farmer's family, servants, and cattle during at least a large part of the first year of his tenancy, or until he can get some return from the land. The annual expenses consist of seed, the wear and tear on farming tools, and the yearly upkeep of the farmer's servants and cattle, and of his family too, so far as any of them can be counted as servants employed in cultivation. The part of the land's produce that remains to him after paying the rent ought to be enough, first, to repay him within a reasonable time, at least during his tenancy, the whole of his original expenses together with the ordinary profits of stock; and, second, to repay him each year the whole of his annual expenses, again together with the ordinary profits of stock. These two kinds of expense are two capitals that the farmer employs in cultivation. Unless they are regularly returned to him along with a reasonable profit, he cannot carry on his business on equal terms with other businesses; and, looking to his own interest, he must abandon it as soon as he can and seek some other. The part of the land's produce that is thus needed to let the farmer continue his business ought to be regarded as a fund set aside and sacred to cultivation. If the landlord violates it, he necessarily reduces the produce of his own land, and within a few years he leaves the farmer unable not only to pay this excessive rent but even to pay the reasonable rent he might otherwise have got for the land. The rent that properly belongs to the landlord is no more than the net produce left over after fully paying all the necessary expenses that must first be laid out in order to raise the gross or total produce. It is because the cultivators' labour, over and above completely covering all those necessary expenses, yields a net produce of this kind that this system singles out this class of people with the honourable name of the productive class. For the same reason their original and annual expenses are called, in this system, productive expenses, because, beyond replacing their own value, they bring about the yearly reproduction of this net produce.

The ground expenses, as they are called, or what the landlord spends on improving his land, are in this system also honoured with the name of productive expenses. Until the whole of those expenses, together with the ordinary profits of stock, have been completely repaid to him through the higher rent he gets from his land, that higher rent ought to be treated as sacred and inviolable by both the church and the king, and ought to be subject neither to tithe nor to taxation. Otherwise, by discouraging the improvement of land, the church discourages the future growth of her own tithes, and the king the future growth of his own taxes. So, in a well-ordered state of things, since these ground expenses not only reproduce their own value completely but also, after a certain time, bring about the reproduction of a net produce, this system counts them as productive expenses.

The landlord's ground expenses, however, together with the farmer's original and annual expenses, are the only three kinds of expense that this system counts as productive. All other expenses, and all other orders of people, even those whom ordinary people regard as the most productive, are treated in this account as wholly barren and unproductive.

Artisans and manufacturers in particular, whose work, in ordinary people's view, adds so much to the value of the raw produce of land, are represented in this system as a class wholly barren and unproductive. Their labour, it is said, only replaces the stock that employs them, together with its ordinary profits. That stock consists of the materials, tools, and wages advanced to them by their employer; it is the fund set aside for their employment and upkeep. Its profits are the fund set aside for the upkeep of their employer. As the employer advances to them the stock of materials, tools, and wages they need for their work, so he also advances to himself what he needs for his own upkeep; and he generally sets that upkeep in proportion to the profit he expects to make from the price of their work. Unless the price repays him both the upkeep he advances to himself and the materials, tools, and wages he advances to his workmen, it clearly does not repay him the whole expense he lays out on it. So the profits of manufacturing stock are not, like the rent of land, a net produce that remains after fully repaying the whole expense that must be laid out in order to obtain it. The farmer's stock yields him a profit, just as the master manufacturer's does; and it also yields a rent to another person, which the master manufacturer's stock does not. The expense laid out in employing and maintaining artisans and manufacturers therefore does no more than keep its own value in existence, so to speak, and produces no new value. It is therefore an altogether barren and unproductive expense. The expense laid out in employing farmers and country labourers, by contrast, not only keeps its own value in existence but produces a new value, the landlord's rent. It is therefore a productive expense.

Mercantile stock is just as barren and unproductive as manufacturing stock. It merely keeps its own value in existence, without producing any new value. Its profits are only the repayment of the upkeep that its employer advances to himself during the time he employs it, or until he gets the returns from it. They are only the repayment of part of the expense that must be laid out in employing it.

The labour of artisans and manufacturers never adds anything to the value of the whole yearly amount of the land's raw produce. It does, indeed, add a great deal to the value of certain particular parts of it. But the consumption it causes of other parts in the meantime is exactly equal to the value it adds to those parts, so that the value of the whole amount is not, at any single moment, increased in the least by it. The person who makes the lace for a pair of fine ruffles, for example, will sometimes raise the value of perhaps a pennyworth of flax to £30 sterling. But although at first glance he seems thereby to multiply the value of part of the raw produce about seven thousand two hundred times, he in fact adds nothing to the value of the whole yearly amount of the raw produce. Making that lace costs him perhaps two years' labour. The £30 he gets for it when it is finished is no more than the repayment of the subsistence he advances to himself during the two years he spends on it. The value he adds to the flax by each day's, month's, or year's labour does no more than replace the value of his own consumption during that day, month, or year. So at no moment does he add anything to the value of the whole yearly amount of the land's raw produce: the portion of that produce he is continually consuming is always equal to the value he is continually producing. The extreme poverty of most of the people employed in this expensive though trifling manufacture may convince us that the price of their work does not, in the usual case, exceed the value of their subsistence. It is otherwise with the work of farmers and country labourers. The landlord's rent is a value that, in the usual case, their work is continually producing over and above completely replacing the whole consumption, the whole expense laid out on employing and maintaining both the workmen and their employer.

Artisans, manufacturers, and merchants can increase the revenue and wealth of their society only by thrift, or, as this system puts it, by privation, that is, by depriving themselves of part of the funds set aside for their own subsistence. Each year they reproduce nothing but those funds. So unless they save some part of them each year, unless they deny themselves the enjoyment of some part of them each year, the revenue and wealth of their society can never be increased in the slightest by their work. Farmers and country labourers, by contrast, can fully enjoy all the funds set aside for their own subsistence and yet at the same time increase the revenue and wealth of their society. Over and above what is set aside for their own subsistence, their work yields each year a net produce, and any growth in it necessarily increases the revenue and wealth of their society. So nations that, like France or England, consist largely of proprietors and cultivators can be enriched both by work and by enjoyment. Nations that, like Holland and Hamburg, are made up chiefly of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers can grow rich only through thrift and privation. Because the interests of nations in such different situations are very different, so too is the common character of the people. In nations of the first kind, generosity, frankness, and good fellowship naturally form part of the common character; in those of the second kind, narrowness, meanness, and a selfish disposition averse to all social pleasure and enjoyment.

The unproductive class, that of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers, is wholly maintained and employed at the expense of the other two classes, the proprietors and the cultivators. These supply it with both the materials of its work and the fund of its subsistence, the corn and cattle it consumes while it is engaged in that work. In the end the proprietors and cultivators pay both the wages of all the workmen of the unproductive class and the profits of all their employers. Those workmen and their employers are really the servants of the proprietors and cultivators. They are merely servants who work out of doors, as menial servants work indoors. Both, however, are equally maintained at the expense of the same masters. The labour of both is equally unproductive. It adds nothing to the value of the total raw produce of the land. Instead of increasing the value of that total, it is a charge and an expense that has to be paid out of it.

The unproductive class, however, is not just useful but greatly useful to the other two classes. Through the work of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers, the proprietors and cultivators can buy both the foreign goods and the manufactured produce of their own country that they need, using the produce of far less of their own labour than they would have to spend if they tried, in a clumsy and unskilled way, either to import the one or to make the other for their own use. Through the unproductive class, the cultivators are freed from many cares that would otherwise distract their attention from cultivating the land. The greater produce they are able to raise as a result of this undivided attention is more than enough to pay the whole cost that maintaining and employing the unproductive class imposes on either the proprietors or themselves. So the work of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers, though in its own nature wholly unproductive, contributes in this way indirectly to increasing the produce of the land. It increases the productive powers of productive labour by leaving it free to confine itself to its proper task, the cultivation of land; and the plough often goes the easier and the better thanks to the labour of the man whose business is most remote from the plough.

It can never be in the interest of the proprietors and cultivators to restrain or discourage in any way the work of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers. The greater the freedom this unproductive class enjoys, the greater the competition will be in all the different trades that make it up, and the more cheaply the other two classes will be supplied with both foreign goods and the manufactured produce of their own country.

It can never be in the interest of the unproductive class to oppress the other two classes. It is the surplus produce of the land, what remains after subtracting the upkeep first of the cultivators and then of the proprietors, that maintains and employs the unproductive class. The greater this surplus, the greater the maintenance and employment of that class must likewise be. Establishing perfect justice, perfect liberty, and perfect equality is the very simple secret that most effectively secures the highest degree of prosperity for all three classes.

The merchants, artisans, and manufacturers of those mercantile states that, like Holland and Hamburg, consist chiefly of this unproductive class are in the same way wholly maintained and employed at the expense of the proprietors and cultivators of land. The only difference is that most of those proprietors and cultivators are placed at a most inconvenient distance from the merchants, artisans, and manufacturers they supply with the materials of their work and the fund of their subsistence: they are inhabitants of other countries and subjects of other governments.

Such mercantile states, however, are not merely useful but greatly useful to the inhabitants of those other countries. They fill, to some extent, a very important gap, and take the place of the merchants, artisans, and manufacturers that the inhabitants of those countries ought to find at home, but, through some flaw in their policy, do not find at home.

It can never be in the interest of those landed nations, if I may call them that, to discourage or distress the work of such mercantile states by imposing high duties on their trade or on the goods they supply. By making those goods dearer, such duties could only sink the real value of the surplus produce of the landed nations' own land, with which, or, what amounts to the same thing, with the price of which, those goods are bought. Such duties could only serve to discourage the growth of that surplus produce, and consequently the improvement and cultivation of their own land. The most effective course, on the contrary, for raising the value of that surplus produce, for encouraging its growth, and so for improving and cultivating their own land, would be to allow the most perfect freedom to the trade of all such mercantile nations.

This perfect freedom of trade would even be the most effective means of supplying them, in due course, with all the artisans, manufacturers, and merchants they lacked at home, and of filling, in the most fitting and advantageous way, that very important gap they felt there.

The continual growth of the surplus produce of their land would, in due course, create a greater capital than could be employed at the ordinary rate of profit in improving and cultivating land; and the surplus part of it would naturally turn to employing artisans and manufacturers at home. But these artisans and manufacturers, finding at home both the materials of their work and the fund of their subsistence, might at once, even with far less art and skill, be able to work as cheaply as the small-scale artisans and manufacturers of such mercantile states, who had to bring both from a greater distance. Even if, for lack of art and skill, they could not for a time work as cheaply, yet, having a market at home, they might be able to sell their work there as cheaply as that of the artisans and manufacturers of such mercantile states, which could be brought to that market only from so great a distance; and as their art and skill improved, they would soon be able to sell it more cheaply. So the artisans and manufacturers of such mercantile states would at once meet rivals in the market of those landed nations, and soon after be undersold and pushed out of it altogether. The cheapness of the manufactures of those landed nations, resulting from the gradual improvement of art and skill, would in due course extend their sales beyond the home market and carry them to many foreign markets, from which they would, in the same way, gradually push out many of the manufacturers of such mercantile nations.

This continual growth, in both the raw and the manufactured produce of those landed nations, would in due course create a greater capital than could be employed, at the ordinary rate of profit, either in agriculture or in manufactures. The surplus of this capital would naturally turn to foreign trade and be used to export to foreign countries whatever parts of the raw and manufactured produce of its own country exceeded the demand of the home market. In exporting the produce of their own country, the merchants of a landed nation would have an advantage of the same kind over those of mercantile nations as its artisans and manufacturers had over the artisans and manufacturers of such nations: the advantage of finding at home the cargo, and the stores and provisions, that the others were obliged to seek from a distance. So, even with inferior art and skill in navigation, they would be able to sell that cargo as cheaply in foreign markets as the merchants of such mercantile nations, and with equal art and skill they would be able to sell it more cheaply. They would therefore soon rival those mercantile nations in this branch of foreign trade, and in due course push them out of it altogether.

According to this liberal and generous system, then, the most advantageous way for a landed nation to raise up artisans, manufacturers, and merchants of its own is to grant the most perfect freedom of trade to the artisans, manufacturers, and merchants of all other nations. In this way it raises the value of the surplus produce of its own land, whose continual growth gradually builds up a fund that, in due course, necessarily raises up all the artisans, manufacturers, and merchants it needs.

When a landed nation, on the contrary, oppresses the trade of foreign nations, whether by high duties or by outright bans, it necessarily harms its own interest in two ways. First, by raising the price of all foreign goods and all kinds of manufactures, it necessarily sinks the real value of the surplus produce of its own land, with which, or, what amounts to the same thing, with the price of which, it buys those foreign goods and manufactures. Second, by giving its own merchants, artisans, and manufacturers a kind of monopoly of the home market, it raises the rate of mercantile and manufacturing profit relative to that of agricultural profit, and consequently either draws away from agriculture part of the capital that had been employed in it, or stops part of what would otherwise have gone to it from going there. So this policy discourages agriculture in two ways: first, by sinking the real value of its produce and thereby lowering the rate of its profits; and, second, by raising the rate of profit in all other occupations. Agriculture is made less advantageous, and trade and manufactures more advantageous, than they otherwise would be; and every man is tempted by his own interest to turn as much of his capital and his work as he can away from the former and toward the latter.

Even supposing this oppressive policy enabled a landed nation to raise up artisans, manufacturers, and merchants of its own somewhat sooner than it could through freedom of trade, which is itself far from certain, it would still raise them up, so to speak, prematurely, before the nation was fully ready for them. By raising up one kind of industry too hastily, it would depress another, more valuable kind. By raising up too hastily a kind of industry that merely replaces the stock that employs it, together with the ordinary profit, it would depress a kind of industry that, beyond replacing that stock with its profit, also yields a net produce, a free rent to the landlord. It would depress productive labour by encouraging too hastily that labour which is wholly barren and unproductive.

How, according to this system, the total yearly produce of the land is distributed among the three classes mentioned above, and how the labour of the unproductive class does no more than replace the value of its own consumption without increasing in any way the value of that total, is set out by Mr Quesnay, the very ingenious and profound author of this system, in some arithmetical tables. The first of these, which he singles out by way of distinction with the name of the Economical Table, shows the way he supposes this distribution to take place in a state of the most perfect liberty, and therefore of the highest prosperity; a state in which the yearly produce is such as to afford the greatest possible net produce, and in which each class enjoys its proper share of the whole yearly produce. Some later tables show the way he supposes this distribution is made under various states of restraint and regulation, in which either the class of proprietors or the barren and unproductive class is favoured more than the class of cultivators, and in which one or the other encroaches, more or less, on the share that ought properly to belong to this productive class. According to this system, every such encroachment, every violation of the natural distribution that perfect liberty would establish, must necessarily degrade, more or less, from one year to the next, the value and total of the yearly produce, and must necessarily cause a gradual decline in the real wealth and revenue of society; a decline whose progress must be quicker or slower according to the degree of the encroachment, according as the natural distribution that perfect liberty would establish is more or less violated. Those later tables show the different degrees of decline that, according to this system, correspond to the different degrees in which this natural distribution of things is violated.

Some speculative physicians seem to have imagined that the health of the human body could be preserved only by a certain precise regimen of diet and exercise, and that every violation of it, however small, necessarily caused some degree of disease or disorder in proportion to the violation. Experience, however, seems to show that the human body often keeps, to all appearances at least, the most perfect state of health under a vast variety of different regimens, even some generally believed to be very far from wholesome. The healthy human body, it seems, contains within itself some unknown principle of preservation, able in many respects either to prevent or to correct the bad effects even of a very faulty regimen. Mr Quesnay, who was himself a physician, and a very speculative one, seems to have held a notion of the same kind about the body politic, imagining that it would thrive and prosper only under a certain precise regimen, the exact regimen of perfect liberty and perfect justice. He seems not to have considered that in the body politic the natural effort each man is continually making to better his own condition is a principle of preservation, able in many respects to prevent and correct the bad effects of a political economy that is to some degree both partial and oppressive. Such a political economy, though it no doubt retards more or less, is not always able to halt altogether the natural progress of a nation toward wealth and prosperity, and still less able to make it go backwards. If a nation could not prosper without enjoying perfect liberty and perfect justice, there is not a nation in the world that could ever have prospered. In the body politic, however, the wisdom of nature has fortunately made ample provision for remedying many of the bad effects of the folly and injustice of man, just as it has done in the natural body for remedying those of his sloth and intemperance.

The fundamental error of this system, however, seems to lie in its treating the class of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants as wholly barren and unproductive. The following observations may serve to show how improper this representation is:—

First, this class, it is acknowledged, reproduces each year the value of its own yearly consumption, and at least keeps in existence the stock or capital that maintains and employs it. But on that ground alone the name barren or unproductive seems very improperly applied to it. We would not call a marriage barren or unproductive even if it produced only a son and a daughter to replace the father and mother, and did not increase the number of the human species but only kept it as it was before. Farmers and country labourers, it is true, over and above the stock that maintains and employs them, reproduce each year a net produce, a free rent for the landlord. Just as a marriage that yields three children is certainly more productive than one that yields only two, so the labour of farmers and country labourers is certainly more productive than that of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers. But the greater produce of the one class does not make the other barren or unproductive.

Second, on this same ground it seems altogether improper to regard artisans, manufacturers, and merchants in the same light as menial servants. The labour of menial servants does not keep in existence the fund that maintains and employs them. Their upkeep and employment is wholly at their masters' expense, and the work they do is not of a kind to repay that expense. That work consists in services that generally perish in the very instant they are performed, and does not fix or realize itself in any saleable commodity that can replace the value of their wages and upkeep. The labour of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants, by contrast, naturally does fix and realize itself in some such saleable commodity. It is on this account that, in the chapter where I deal with productive and unproductive labour, I have classed artisans, manufacturers, and merchants among the productive labourers, and menial servants among the barren or unproductive.

Third, on every supposition it seems improper to say that the labour of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants does not increase the real revenue of society. Even if we supposed, as this system seems to suppose, that the value of this class's daily, monthly, and yearly consumption was exactly equal to that of its daily, monthly, and yearly production, it would not follow that its labour added nothing to the real revenue, to the real value of the yearly produce of the land and labour of society. An artisan, for example, who in the first six months after harvest does ten pounds' worth of work, even though in the same time he consumes ten pounds' worth of corn and other necessaries, really adds ten pounds of value to the yearly produce of the land and labour of society. While he has been consuming a half-yearly revenue of ten pounds' worth of corn and other necessaries, he has produced an equal value of work, able to buy, either for himself or for someone else, an equal half-yearly revenue. So the value of what has been consumed and produced during these six months is equal not to ten but to twenty pounds. It is possible, indeed, that no more than ten pounds' worth of this value ever existed at any single moment. But if the ten pounds' worth of corn and other necessaries consumed by the artisan had instead been consumed by a soldier or a menial servant, the value of that part of the yearly produce existing at the end of the six months would have been ten pounds less than it actually is thanks to the artisan's labour. So even though the value of what the artisan produces is supposed never, at any single moment, to be greater than the value he consumes, yet at every moment the value of goods actually existing in the market is, because of what he produces, greater than it otherwise would be.

When the supporters of this system claim that the consumption of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants is equal to the value of what they produce, they probably mean no more than that their revenue, or the fund set aside for their consumption, is equal to it. But if they had expressed themselves more accurately, and claimed only that the revenue of this class was equal to the value of what it produced, the reader might readily have noticed that whatever was naturally saved out of this revenue must necessarily increase, more or less, the real wealth of society. So in order to construct something like an argument, they had to express themselves as they did; and this argument, even granting that things were as it seems to assume, turns out to be a very weak one.

Fourth, farmers and country labourers can no more increase, without thrift, the real revenue, the yearly produce of the land and labour of their society, than artisans, manufacturers, and merchants can. The yearly produce of the land and labour of any society can be increased in only two ways: first, by some improvement in the productive powers of the useful labour actually maintained within it; or, second, by some increase in the quantity of that labour.

The improvement in the productive powers of useful labour depends, first, on improvement in the workman's skill, and, second, on improvement in the machinery he works with. But the labour of artisans and manufacturers, since it can be more finely subdivided, and the labour of each workman reduced to a greater simplicity of operation, than that of farmers and country labourers, is likewise capable of both these kinds of improvement to a much higher degree (see book i, chap. 1). In this respect, therefore, the class of cultivators can have no sort of advantage over that of artisans and manufacturers.

How much useful labour a society actually employs depends entirely on how much its capital grows, and that capital can grow only by exactly the amount saved out of revenue—whether saved by the people who manage and direct the capital themselves, or by others who lend it to them. This system assumes that merchants, craftsmen, and manufacturers are naturally more thrifty and more inclined to save than landowners and farmers. If that is true, then to that extent they are the ones more likely to expand the useful labour employed in their society, and so to increase its real revenue, which is the yearly output of its land and labour.

Fifth and finally: even if we grant this system's assumption that a country's revenue consists entirely of the amount of subsistence its industry can secure, a trading and manufacturing country must still always be far richer than one without trade or manufactures, all else being equal. Trade and manufactures let a country import more subsistence each year than its own land, cultivated as it currently is, could supply. Townspeople often own no land at all, yet through their industry they draw to themselves enough of the raw produce of other people's land to supply both the materials of their work and the fund that feeds them. What a town always is to the countryside around it, one independent state can often be to other independent states. This is how Holland draws much of its food from abroad—live cattle from Holstein and Jutland, and grain from almost every country in Europe. A small amount of manufactured goods buys a large amount of raw produce. So a trading and manufacturing country naturally uses a small part of its manufactured output to buy a large part of the raw produce of other countries, while a country without trade or manufactures must usually give up a large part of its raw produce to buy only a tiny part of other countries' manufactured goods. The first exports what can support and supply only a few people, and imports the support and supply of many. The second exports the support and supply of many, and imports that of only a few. The people of the first must always enjoy far more subsistence than their own land, as currently cultivated, could provide. The people of the second must always enjoy far less.

Still, for all its flaws, this system is perhaps the closest approach to the truth yet published on the subject of political economy, and for that reason it deserves the attention of anyone who wants to study the principles of that very important science carefully. Its claim that only labour applied to land is productive is, admittedly, too narrow and cramped. But when it says that the wealth of nations lies not in the useless hoard of money but in the consumable goods that the society's labour reproduces each year, and when it says that perfect liberty is the only effective way to make that yearly reproduction as large as possible, its doctrine seems entirely as sound as it is generous and liberal. Its followers are very numerous.
